Alabama

Alabama people have southeastern homelands and enduring communities in Texas and Oklahoma. Their history intersects closely with Coushatta people and the Creek Confederacy, but Alabama is also a distinct language and historical identity. The Alabama-Coushatta Tribe of Texas and Alabama-Quassarte Tribal Town provide different contemporary settings for understanding that continuity.

An expanded introduction, with sources reviewed.This profile develops several themes through identified sources. Citations connect each section to its evidence; remaining gaps appear below. It has not been reviewed or endorsed by the community.
01

A people, a language, and several political histories

Alabama names an Indigenous people rather than all Native peoples living within the present state of Alabama. Colonial records locate Alabama and Quassarte communities along the Alabama River, whose name also became the state's name. Their languages belong to the Muskogean family, and extensive intermarriage linked the communities. These connections help explain shared institutions, but they should not erase distinctions between Alabama, Coushatta/Quassarte, and Muscogee identities or turn present governments into interchangeable names.

Read the sources [3] Oklahoma Historical Society; John H. Moore [4] Alabama Quassarte Tribal Town

02

Migration and the Texas homeland

The Texas tribe's own history describes migration from adjacent southeastern territories into East Texas during the late eighteenth century. Alabama and Coushatta communities established villages across what became Polk, Tyler, and San Jacinto counties. Their history includes diplomacy and assistance to Sam Houston's forces and refugees during the 1836 Texas Revolution. The present reservation in the Big Thicket represents a long process of settlement and political negotiation, rather than the full extent of the people's earlier homelands.

Read the sources [1] Alabama-Coushatta Tribe of Texas [2] Alabama-Coushatta Tribe of Texas

03

Removal and Alabama-Quassarte in Oklahoma

Other Alabama and Quassarte people remained associated with the Creek Confederacy and were forcibly removed to Indian Territory in the nineteenth century. Alabama-Quassarte Tribal Town describes that removal as part of its own community history and identifies its 1939 constitution as the foundation for its modern government. Its headquarters are at Wetumka, Oklahoma. The town's distinct sovereignty and its Muscogee historical relationships belong together; neither makes it simply an Oklahoma branch administered by the Texas tribe.

Read the sources [3] Oklahoma Historical Society; John H. Moore [4] Alabama Quassarte Tribal Town

04

Government and community continuity

The Alabama-Coushatta Tribe of Texas describes an elected Tribal Council, advisory chiefly offices, and community services including health care, law enforcement, and emergency response. Its timeline records restoration of federal recognition in 1987. Alabama-Quassarte likewise identifies self-government, tribal law, education, housing, and member services as expressions of sovereignty. These accounts show that Alabama history continues through operating governments and community institutions, alongside ceremonial and family relationships, rather than ending with migration or removal.

Read the sources [1] Alabama-Coushatta Tribe of Texas [4] Alabama Quassarte Tribal Town

05

Alabama language documentation and learning

The Alabama Dictionary Online is a collaboration between the Texas tribe and Harvard's WOLF Lab, building on work by Cora Sylestine, Heather Hardy, and Thomas Montler. It combines searchable vocabulary, grammatical information, speaker recordings, and lessons; speakers approve recordings and collected material is shared with and owned by the tribe. Harvard's September 2026 report describes workshops with elders and weekly online instruction, including paid learning time approved for tribal employees. These are specific community-directed language activities, not evidence that the Alabama people have disappeared.

Read the sources [5] Alabama-Coushatta Tribe of Texas and WOLF Lab collaborative project [6] Harvard University Department of Linguistics
